q: What is servant leadership, which PMI's agile guide calls supportive leadership?
options: Leading through service to the team, meeting team members' needs so the team can perform at its best
Leading only when the team asks
Leading by doing the team's work personally
explanation: Supportive leadership is the practice of leading through service to the team, focusing on the needs and development of team members to enable the highest possible team performance.

q: In which order does a servant leader approach project work?
explanation: First the purpose (the why), then the people (an environment where everyone can succeed), then the process (look for results, not a perfect process).

q: A team delivers working product every two weeks, but each release then waits six weeks in another department's approval queue. What should the servant leader do?
options: Work with that department to streamline the process and remove the impediment
Tell the team to work faster
Lengthen the sprints to eight weeks
explanation: Servant leaders remove organizational impediments. They look at processes that are lengthy and cause bottlenecks, and work with others to streamline them.

q: Which of the following is a characteristic of servant leadership?
options: Controlling how each task is done
Making all decisions for the team
explanation: Characteristics include listening, serving the team, helping people grow, coaching versus controlling, and promoting safety, respect and trust.

q: When a project manager acts as a servant leader, how does the emphasis change?
options: From serving the team to directing it
From managing coordination to facilitating collaboration
From delivering value to writing detailed progress reports
explanation: The emphasis shifts from managing coordination to facilitating collaboration. Facilitators help everyone do their best thinking and work.

q: How does the project manager's position change in an agile environment?
options: The project manager makes every technical decision on the team's behalf
The project manager assigns all tasks daily
From being at the center of coordination to supporting the team
The project manager replaces the product owner
explanation: On an agile project, project managers shift from being at the center to supporting the team, coaching, fostering collaboration and aligning stakeholder needs.

q: What is the typical size of the most effective agile teams?
explanation: The most effective agile teams tend to range from three to nine members, which keeps communication manageable without formal structures.

q: A new manager on an agile project starts handing each developer a task every morning, and the team objects. In a self-organizing team, who decides which team member does which piece of work?
explanation: Agile encourages self-managing teams, where team members decide who will perform the work within the next period's scope.

q: A tester can also write code for some parts of the product and helps wherever work is stuck. What kind of skills does this person have?
explanation: A T-shaped person, or generalizing specialist, has a focused specialty plus supporting skills in other areas and good collaboration skills.

q: A manager praises the developer who closes the most tasks each week, while finished work piles up waiting for the one tester. Why can focusing on one person's individual output be harmful to an agile team?
options: Because individuals should not work hard
Because it can create a bottleneck; what matters is the throughput of the whole team
Because only the product owner's output matters when the increment is reviewed by sponsors
explanation: A single person's throughput is not relevant and may be harmful if it creates a bottleneck. The goal is flow efficiency: optimizing the delivery of finished work by the team.

q: A team member is assigned 50% to project A and 50% to project B. According to PMI's agile guide, how much are they effectively dedicated to each?
explanation: Because of the cost of task-switching, a person multitasking between two projects is only 20% to 40% dedicated to each, not 50%.

q: A developer is split between three projects and loses hours every day switching from one to another. What is the main benefit of having team members 100% dedicated to one team?
options: The fastest possible throughput, with no time lost to task-switching
explanation: When people are 100% dedicated to the team, the team has the fastest possible throughput. Multitasking slows the whole team and causes more mistakes.

q: What is psychological safety?
options: A guarantee that nobody will be laid off
A shared belief that the team is a safe place to speak up, ask questions and admit mistakes without fear
A rule that disagreements are not allowed
explanation: Psychological safety is a shared belief that the environment is safe for interpersonal risk-taking, without fear of embarrassment or retaliation.

q: A junior developer feels able to say, in front of the whole team, that the agreed design is wrong and to propose another. In the four stages of psychological safety, which stage lets people question assumptions and suggest changes without fear?
explanation: The stages are inclusion, learner, contributor and challenger safety. Challenger safety, the last, enables innovation and continuous improvement.

q: A team stays silent in its retrospectives because people are afraid of being blamed. How can its leader best strengthen psychological safety?
options: By admitting their own mistakes, asking for help and responding to feedback without defensiveness
By criticizing mistakes in front of the team
By cancelling retrospectives to save time
explanation: Leaders strengthen psychological safety by modeling vulnerability, admitting uncertainty, sharing mistakes and responding constructively to challenge.

q: Inside a two-week iteration, a team first writes all the requirements, then does all the design, then all the building. Late in the iteration it finds its assumptions were wrong. What is this pattern called?
explanation: Mini-waterfalls occur when the team does all of one kind of work before the next. Collaborating on a small number of features end to end lets the team learn as it goes.

q: Several team members stop their own tasks to work together on one blocked item until it is finished. What is this called?
explanation: Swarming is several team members focusing together on one item to get it finished. It limits work in progress and speeds up flow.

q: Which of the three common agile roles ranks the work by business value?
explanation: The product owner is responsible for guiding the direction of the product and ranks the work based on its business value.

q: A developer tells the team facilitator that a missing software license has blocked her for two days. What should the facilitator do?
options: Work to get the impediment removed so she can continue
Tell her to solve it herself
Reassign all of her tasks to someone else on the same team
Report her to her line manager
explanation: Removing impediments and paving the way for the team's work are core responsibilities of a servant leader.

q: What is the difference between a distributed team and a dispersed team?
options: A distributed team works in one room; a dispersed team in two rooms
A dispersed team has no product owner
Distributed: cross-functional teams in different locations. Dispersed: each team member in a different location.
explanation: Distributed teams employ cross-functional teams in different locations. Dispersed teams may have each member working in a different location.

q: In a shared team room, a developer overhears two colleagues discussing a problem and offers the solution. What is this kind of information flow called?
explanation: Osmotic communication is picking up useful information by overhearing teammates who work in the same space.

q: Which condition is a threat to psychological safety?
options: A working agreement written and regularly reviewed by the whole team
Public criticism and blame when someone raises a problem
A leader who asks for help
explanation: Behaviors that shame or punish people for speaking up, including public criticism and assigning blame, discourage open communication.
